'''''Aquilegia alpina''''', often called the '''alpine columbine''' or '''breath of God''',<ref name="RHS"/> is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Ranunculaceae]], native to the western and central Alps.<ref name="POWO"/> Though rare in its Swiss, Austrian, and Italian range, it is commonly found in the French [[Maritime Alps]]. ''A. alpina'' is appreciated for its light blue to blue-purple flowers.

The species has been in cultivation for several centuries, but plants sold as ''A. alpina'' are often hybrids with other ''Aquilegia'' species or different columbine species entirely. True ''A. alpina'' plants possess straight or slightly curved [[nectar spur]]s, distinguishing it from other species and hybrids with hooked spurs. At {{cvt|21.5|mm}} long, these spurs are the longest of any Eurasian member of the genus ''[[Aquilegia]]''.

==Description==
''Aquilegia alpina'' is a [[perennial]] that grows to between {{cvt|15|cm}} and {{cvt|60|cm}} tall.<ref name="POWO"/><ref name=Nold>{{cite book|title=Columbines: ''Aquilegia'', ''Paraquilegia'', and ''Semiaquilegia''|first=Robert|last=Nold|publisher=Timber Press|date=2003|location=[[Portland, Oregon|Portland]], [[Oregon|OR]]|isbn=0-88192-588-8|url=https://archive.org/details/columbines00robe/mode/1up|via=[[Internet Archive]]|url-access=registration}}</ref>{{rp|62}} Leaves are biternate and in a basal arrange (growing from the base of the stem). The lower portions of the stems are pilose and the upper portions are densely pubescent.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|62}} The middle [[leaflet (botany)|leaflet]]s are between {{cvt|22|mm}} and {{cvt|28|mm}} long and between {{cvt|24|mm}} and {{cvt|34|mm}} wide. They are petioluled.<ref name=Skalińska>{{cite journal|title=Studies in ''Aquilegia''|first=Maria|last=Skalińska|author-link=Maria Skalińska|journal=Proceedings of the Linnean Society of London|publisher=[[Linnean Society of London]]}}</ref>{{rp|331}}

Plants feature between one and three (occasionally up to 5) flowers per stem.<ref name="GBIF"/> Each flower is nodding.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|62}} The flowers are bright light blue to blue-purple, measuring {{cvt|6–9|cm}} across. The species's [[nectar spur]]s at the tip of the flower is straight or only slightly curved,<ref name="GBIF"/> and are the longest of the Eurasian species of ''[[Aquilegia]]'' at {{cvt|21.5|mm}}.<ref name="Whittall"/> The spreading [[sepal]]s range in shape from lance-ovate to wider and are between {{cvt|3|cm}} and {{cvt|4.5|cm}} long.<ref name=Munz>{{cite book|title=Aquilegia: The Cultivated and Wild Columbines|series=Gentes Herbarum|volume=VII|location=[[Ithaca, New York|Ithaca]], [[New York (state)|NY]]|author-link=Philip A. Munz|first=Philip A.|last=Munz|date=March 25, 1946|publisher=[[New York State College of Agriculture and Life Sciences at Cornell University|The Bailey Hortorium of the New York State College of Agriculture at Cornell University]]|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_gentes-herbarum_1946-03-25_7_1|via=Archive.org}}</ref>{{rp|85}}

The plant's flowers are considered to possess unusual beauty. Robert Nold described the American botanist [[Philip A. Munz]] as having "almost broke down completely" when Munz described ''A. alpina'' as "one of the most beautiful of all the ''Aquilegias''". The British botanist [[Reginald Farrer]] was similarly appreciative of the flower's appearance.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|62}}

==Taxonomy==
The species was first described as ''Aquilegia alpina'' in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his ''[[Species Plantarum]]''. He described the [[type locality (biology)|type locality]] as [[Switzerland]].<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|62}}

In 1882, a specimen was identified as a variant of ''[[Isopyrum thalictroides]]'' and given the name ''I. thalictroides'' var. ''insignis'' by Gibelli and Pirotta. However, this specimen was reevaluated by Maria Adele Signorini and Enio Nardi in 1999 and identified as an example of ''A. alpina''. They attributed this false identification to the absence lack of spurs on the specimen's sole flower. Since the specimen was the [[type specimen]] and only known specimen of ''I. thalictroides'' var. ''insignis'', Signorini and Nardi said that name should be considered a heterotypic nomenclature synonym of ''A. alpina''.<ref name="Signorini"/>

The nectar spurs of ''A. alpina'' are the longest of Eurasian species of ''Aquilegia''. Among these species, nectar spur length varies little and there is no evidence of evolution to exploit [[hawkmoth]] pollination.  ''A. alpina''{{apostrophe}}s spurs are {{cvt|10|mm}} shorter than those of the shortest hawkmoth-pollinated North American member of the genus, ''[[Aquilegia pubescens]]'', which has spurs that can reach {{cvt|32.4|mm}} long. A 2007 study by Justen B. Whittall and Scott A. Hodges attributed this discrepancy in nectar spur length between Eurasian and North American ''Aquilegia'' species despite the presence of hawkmoths in both ranges  to the absence of [[hummingbird]]s in Eurasia. Whittall and Hodges theorized that hummingbirds served as a "stepping stone" to nectar spur elongation adapted to hawkmoth pollination.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature05857|title=Pollinator shifts drive increasingly long nectar spurs in columbine flowers|first1=Justen B.|last1=Whittall|first2=Scott A.|last2=Hodges|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|volume=447|date=2007|issue=7145 |pages=706–709|doi=10.1038/nature05857|pmid=17554306 |bibcode=2007Natur.447..706W |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The word ''[[wikt:columbine|columbine]]'' derives from the Latin word ''[[wikt:columbinus|columbinus]]'', meaning "dove", a reference to the flowers' appearance of a group of doves. The genus name ''[[wikt:Aquilegia|Aquilegia]]'' may come from the Latin word for "eagle", ''[[wikt:aquila|aquila]]'', in reference to the pedals' resemblance to eagle talons.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=AQCHC|title=Aquilegia chrysantha var. chaplinei|website=wildflower.org|publisher=[[Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center]]|access-date=January 16, 2025|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20240613052630/https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=AQCHC|archive-date=June 13, 2024|url-status=live}}</ref> ''Aquilegia'' may also derive from {{lang|la|aquam legere}}, which is Latin for "to collect water", or ''[[wikt:aquilegium|aquilegium]]'', a Latin word for a container of water.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dryades.units.it/Grappa/index.php?procedure=taxon_page&id=10000042&num=30877|title=Aquilegia confusa Rota|work=Portale alla flora del Monte Grappa|publisher=[[University of Trieste]]|access-date=January 16, 2025|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20241210035437/https://dryades.units.it/Grappa/index.php?procedure=taxon_page&id=10000042&num=30877|archive-date=December 10, 2024|url-status=live|lang=it}}</ref> The specific name ''alpina'' references the plant's native habitat of mountain meadows, as the German word ''Alp'' refers to these meadows.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|62}} The plant has been commonly referred to both as the "alpine columbine" and the "breath of God".<ref name="RHS"/>

==Distribution and habitat==
The species is native to subalpine<ref name="GBIF"/> regions of France, Switzerland, Austria, and Italy,<ref name="POWO"/> at altitudes from {{cvt|1300–1900|m}},<ref name="Skuhravá"/> typically in rocky areas and stony pastures<ref name="Signorini"/> with [[Carbonate rock|carbonate bedrock]].<ref name="Caironi"/> In the subalpine meadows of southwestern Switzerland, Austria, and northwestern Italy, the plant is rare. However, it is present with greater commonality in the [[Maritime Alps]] of France.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|62}}

==Ecology==
''Aquilegia alpina'' flowers from July to September,<ref name="GBIF"/> and is pollinated by bees.<ref name="Whittall"/> Hybrid ''A. alpina'' with hooked nectar spurs that were cultivated in the United States have been observed being foraged by the moth species ''[[Hemaris thysbe]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Foraging Behavior of ''Bombus'' (Hymenoptera: Apidae) in Relation to ''Aquilegia'' Pollination|first=Lazarus Walter|last=Macior|journal=[[American Journal of Botany]]|date=March 1966|volume=53|number=3|page=304|doi=10.2307/2439803|jstor=2439803}}</ref> 

===Pests and diseases===
The flowers are known to be attacked by the [[Cecidomyiidae|gall midge species]] ''[[Macrolabis aquilegiae]]''<ref name="Skuhravá"/> and the aphid ''[[Nasonovia werderi]]''.<ref name="Ellis-2025"/> Most recorded parasites of ''A. alpina'' attack the leaves: the leaf miner ''[[Phytomyza minuscula]]'' and cabbage whitefly ''[[Aleyrodes proletella]]'', the [[oomycete]] ''[[Peronospora aquilegiicola]]'' which causes the disease Aquilegia [[downy mildew]], and the fungi ''[[Erysiphe aquilegiae]]'' var. ''aquilegiae'' (causing [[powdery mildew]]), ''[[Puccinia actaeae-elymi]]'', and ''[[Puccinia agrostidis]]''.<ref name="Ellis-2025"/>

==Conservation==
{{As of|2024|October}}, the [[IUCN Red List]] listed ''Aquilegia alpina'' as Least Concern (LC). This status was last reviewed on {{Nowrap|24 June 2010}}.<ref name="IUCN"/> In Switzerland, it is listed as fully protected in the [[Canton of Bern|Bern]], [[Canton of Glarus|Glarus]], [[Grisons]], [[Obwalden]], [[Ticino]], and [[Canton of Uri|Uri]] [[Cantons of Switzerland|cantons]].<ref name="GBIF"/>

==Cultivation==
''Aquilegia alpina'' has a long history of cultivation and was a common offering by 1946.<ref name=Munz/>{{rp|87}} Most plants sold as ''A alpina'' are instead crosses between multiple ''Aquilegia'' species, a phenomenon common across the genus and the result of hundreds of years of cultivation. By 1946, Munz said that supposed "''A. alpina''" plants were generally hybridizations incorporating ''[[Aquilegia vulgaris]]''; this lineage is discernible in the hooked nectar spurs typical of these plants. Other plants labeled ''A. alpina'' were instead ''[[Aquilegia bertolonii]]''.<ref name=Munz/>{{rp|81, 87}}<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|63}} Nold noted that Munz's observations remained true in 2003.<ref name=Nold/>{{rp|63}}
